1.pericope_label: The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel by Malachi. I have loved you, saith the Lord. Yet ye say, Wherein hast thou loved us? Was not Esau Jacob’s brother? saith the Lord: yet I loved Jacob, And I hated Esau, and laid his mountains and his heritage waste for the dragons of the wilderness. Whereas Edom saith, We are impoverished, but we will return and build the desolate places; thus saith the Lord of hosts, They shall build, but I will throw down; and they shall call them, The border of wickedness, and, The people against whom the Lord hath indignation for ever. And your eyes shall see, and ye shall say, The Lord will be magnified from the border of Israel.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch report that the prophet's life is so unknown that it is disputed whether the word in the heading is a name or an ideal title given to the man who foretold the coming messenger; the ancient Greek read it as by the hand of his angel, and the Targumist glossed it with the name of a famous scribe of the return, a conjecture they trace to the spirit of the prophecy rather than evidence. On the last verse they agree with Ellicott that the phrase does not mean beyond the border but simply over or above it. Ellicott glosses the opening verb as having shown abundant proof of love, holds that the nations and not the individuals are in view in the love and the hatred, infers that the subjugation of Edom was by the Babylonian king, prefers jackals to dragons, and prefers the rendering the Lord is great to let him be magnified.

Gill takes the book to be called a burden not because it was heavy to carry or to bear, some of it being matter of joy, but because it was a message sent by the Lord and carried by his servant; he enumerates the proofs of the love, the choosing of them above all people, their continuance through a train of revolutions and their late deliverance; and he calls the hatred of Esau negative rather than positive, yet carries it into the man's own case, that God denied him special grace so that he had no part in the inheritance above. Calvin says those who explain the word burden as prophecy without exception are mistaken, since the word always carries some judgment of God, the ungodly having used it as a proverb of reproach.

Clarke reports the conjecture that the prophet is the famous scribe under a feigned name and adds what can be dated, that this is the last of the Jewish prophets, the temple begun under two predecessors standing complete in his day; on the hatred he denies that a word is spoken of the eternal state of either brother, holding that what is spoken concerns their earthly possessions and the posterity of each rather than the two men; and he refers the throwing down of Edom's rebuilding to two later Jewish rulers. Wesley dates the laying waste five years after the sacking of Jerusalem and adds that the one captivity returned and rebuilt its cities while the other never did.

Henry divides the word burden five ways: weight, repetition, reproach to those weary of it, ruin to the impenitent, and to those who welcome it a burden still, though light. He notes how abruptly the sermon begins, as though God meant, whatever reproofs were coming, to reconcile them to his love first; and he refers the throwing down to a far later attempt of the Jews themselves to rebuild their own city, thrown down by earthquakes and eruptions of fire.

debates.question: What does the word burden mean in the heading?

positions.position: It always carries a judgment of God; those who explain it as prophecy without exception are mistaken.
Not heavy at all, but simply a message sent by the Lord and carried by his servant.
Five senses at once, from weight and repetition to ruin for the impenitent and a light burden for those who welcome it.

debates.question: Does the hatred of Esau bear on the eternal state of the man?

positions.position: Yes: God denied him special grace and left him to his lusts, so that he had no part in the inheritance above.
No: not a word is spoken of the eternal state of either brother, and the passage concerns the posterity of each rather than the two men.
The nations and not the individuals are in view, and the ethical reason for either is not touched on.

debates.question: When was Edom's rebuilding thrown down?

positions.position: The laying waste was by the Babylonian king, five years after the sacking of Jerusalem.
The throwing down was the work of two later Jewish rulers who invaded that country.
It was fulfilled far later, when the Jews themselves attempted to rebuild their own city and were stopped by earthquakes and fire.

outliers.claim: Quotes a modern writer on the evidence of prophecy who sets an ancient historian's description of the country as a bare desert against the cities named in a later age and the ruins reported by travellers, to show that Edom did build the desolate places and that they were afterwards thrown down.

themes: The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel by Malachi.
I have loved you, saith the Lord. Yet ye say, Wherein hast thou loved us? Was not Esau Jacob’s brother? saith the Lord: yet I loved Jacob,
And I hated Esau, and laid his mountains and his heritage waste for the dragons of the wilderness.

Whereas Edom saith, We are impoverished, but we will return and build the desolate places; thus saith the Lord of hosts, They shall build, but I will throw down; and they shall call them, The border of wickedness, and, The people against whom the Lord hath indignation for ever.
And your eyes shall see, and ye shall say, The Lord will be magnified from the border of Israel.

6.pericope_label: A son honoureth his father, and a servant his master: if then I be a father, where is mine honour? and if I be a master, where is my fear? saith the Lord of hosts unto you, O priests, that despise my name. And ye say, Wherein have we despised thy name? Ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar; and ye say, Wherein have we polluted thee? In that ye say, The table of the Lord is contemptible. And if ye offer the blind for sacrifice, is it not evil? and if ye offer the lame and sick, is it not evil? offer it now unto thy governor; will he be pleased with thee, or accept thy person? saith the Lord of hosts.

schools.summary: Ellicott divides the fear required into servile, in which punishment and not fault is dreaded, and filial, in which the fault is feared; on the offering he argues that the word rendered bread means food generally, carries the sense of flesh in a cognate tongue, and is used elsewhere of the fat of the peace offerings; and he rejects Keil's construction of the sentence by name, on the ground that a participial phrase without the article cannot stand parallel to one defined by it. Keil and Delitzsch argue that the clause about offering cannot be the answer to the priests' question, since an answer could not be given in a participle, and read it as parallel to the address to the despisers of God's name.

Gill keeps the plain rendering of the first clause, that a son should honour by the laws of God and of man alike; he follows an ancient writer in taking the polluted bread for the loaves of the presence and goes into the priestly labour of grinding, sifting, kneading and baking; and he reports a Jewish reading in which the priests, given a blind lamb, said it was not evil but good enough to offer, because the table was contemptible.

Clarke supposes the priests took the refuse beasts to ingratiate themselves with the people, bringing the sacrificial ordinances into contempt, and identifies the title of the civil ruler as a foreign term for a lieutenant or viceroy among three neighbouring empires, adding the melancholy note that neither then nor after was there a king in Israel. Wesley puts the charge comparatively: undutifulness in the ignorant might have been excusable, whereas these men, whose business was to know God, despised him as the sons of Eli did and made others do the same.

Henry notes the reversal, that men appointed to call others to account are now called to account themselves, so that rulers in the house of God may know there is one above them; he will not let the charge stay with the priests, since what is said to them is said to all who profess a priesthood; and he grounds the first relation in nature, a son honouring his father because he is his father, that law being written in the hearts of children before it was written on stone, while a servant's obligation is not natural but by compact and yet felt as duty.

debates.question: What is the polluted bread offered on the altar?

positions.position: The loaves of the presence, polluted when not of fine flour or wanting frankincense.
Not the loaves of the presence, which were never offered on the altar, but the sacrificial food itself.
Either the meal offerings or, more largely, everything presented to God.

debates.question: Is the clause about offering polluted bread the answer to the priests' question?

positions.position: No: an answer could not be given in a participle, so the clause is parallel to the address to the despisers of God's name and the answer comes at the words in that ye say.
Yes, and the received version is perfectly correct; the error of the other rendering lies in making an anarthrous participial phrase parallel to one defined by the article.

outliers.claim: Draws from the word used for the civil ruler, a foreign term for a lieutenant or viceroy among three neighbouring empires, the melancholy note that neither at this time nor ever after was there a king in Israel.

themes: A son honoureth his father, and a servant his master: if then I be a father, where is mine honour? and if I be a master, where is my fear? saith the Lord of hosts unto you, O priests, that despise my name. And ye say, Wherein have we despised thy name?
Ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar; and ye say, Wherein have we polluted thee? In that ye say, The table of the Lord is contemptible.

And if ye offer the blind for sacrifice, is it not evil? and if ye offer the lame and sick, is it not evil? offer it now unto thy governor; will he be pleased with thee, or accept thy person? saith the Lord of hosts.

9.pericope_label: And now, I pray you, beseech God that he will be gracious unto us: this hath been by your means: will he regard your persons? saith the Lord of hosts. Who is there even among you that would shut the doors for nought? neither do ye kindle fire on mine altar for nought. I have no pleasure in you, saith the Lord of hosts, neither will I accept an offering at your hand. For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering: for my name shall be great among the heathen, saith the Lord of hosts.

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the appeal to entreat God severely ironical, notes that the name for God is varied to set the divine judge against the human ruler just named, would set the emphasis on the words by your means, and reads the following question as asking not whether God will regard the priests but whether he will on their account show favour to anyone. He rejects the rendering by which the temple might as well be closed, since the word even can only attach to the priests; and on the great name among the nations he argues that the verse has no verb, that taken as present it meets an insurmountable difficulty, and that heathen rites cannot be meant as offered ignorantly to the true God, so the words must be a prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles. Keil and Delitzsch render the verses through without comment.

Gill offers both readings of the appeal without choosing, a genuine exhortation to that part of their office which lay in interceding or a taunt that they should go and intercede and see how they succeed; he reports the Jewish expositors on the shutting of the doors and notes that the words for nothing do not stand where the received version puts them; and he reports the suggestion that the heathen ultimately direct their worship to the supreme Being, rejecting it as flatly as Ellicott does.

Clarke takes the appeal straight, as an exhortation to pray while marks of displeasure lie on the land, and states the conclusion of the eleventh verse without the argument: what is foretold is the abolition of the old sacrifices and a spiritual worship over the whole earth. Wesley takes the word for incense as a legal term for a gospel duty covering prayers, praises and all gospel worship, and reads the pure offering as sincere against hypocrisy and holy against superstition.

Henry finds three senses in the appeal: the ironical one, a real charge to stand in the gap for a land then eaten up with locusts, and a call to repentance, making up by fervency of prayer what was wanting in the worth of their sacrifices. On the shutting of the doors he takes the clause the other way about, as evidence that God does not expect his servants to work for nothing, not a cup of cold water given for his honour losing its reward.

debates.question: Is the call to entreat God serious or ironical?

positions.position: Severely ironical.
Either serious or ironical; both readings are offered without a choice between them.
Three senses at once: ironical, a real charge to intercede for a land under locusts, and a call to repentance.
Straightforward: an exhortation to pray while marks of displeasure lie on the land.

debates.question: What does the verse about shutting the doors mean?

positions.position: A wish that someone would shut the doors of the court against abominable offerings.
The received version stands: not one of them would do the smallest service unpaid; the alternative fails because the word even can only attach to the priests.
Evidence on the other side, that God does not expect his servants to work for nothing.

outliers.claim: Argues that the Hebrew word usually rendered incense is not used elsewhere in that sense and is more naturally rendered shall be burnt, and adds that those who claim the verse for the use of incense in churches must equally keep the yearly feast it is set beside in another prophet, the word pure being emphatic not as marking a bloodless sacrifice but as the converse of polluted.

themes: And now, I pray you, beseech God that he will be gracious unto us: this hath been by your means: will he regard your persons? saith the Lord of hosts.

Who is there even among you that would shut the doors for nought? neither do ye kindle fire on mine altar for nought. I have no pleasure in you, saith the Lord of hosts, neither will I accept an offering at your hand.

For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering: for my name shall be great among the heathen, saith the Lord of hosts.

12.pericope_label: But ye have profaned it, in that ye say, The table of the Lord is polluted; and the fruit thereof, even his meat, is contemptible. Ye said also, Behold, what a weariness is it! and ye have snuffed at it, saith the Lord of hosts; and ye brought that which was torn, and the lame, and the sick; thus ye brought an offering: should I accept this of your hand? saith the Lord. But cursed be the deceiver, which hath in his flock a male, and voweth, and sacrificeth unto the Lord a corrupt thing: for I am a great King, saith the Lord of hosts, and my name is dreadful among the heathen.

schools.summary: Ellicott would put the verb of profaning in the present, reports the Jewish tradition that the pronoun there stands as a euphemism to avoid saying me, and sets the conduct of these priests against the reverence just foretold of the heathen. He renders the gesture of contempt as puffing at the service, and on the word rendered torn shows at length that it means stolen elsewhere, is never used for torn in the later Jewish writings, and is the very word rabbinic tradition uses when naming what is stolen as unfit for a burnt offering.

Gill gives two possibilities for the complaint of weariness, that the words are the priests', complaining of a service for which they thought themselves poorly paid, or the people's, who having carried a lamb on their shoulders said how weary they were with bringing it; and on the closing curse he takes the word for a crafty and subtle man, while recording that some derive it from a root meaning to be able, so that the ancient versions read it of the man who is able to bring a proper offering and does not.

Clarke states the consequence of profaning baldly, that having desecrated the worship they can hardly wonder at being cast off, reads the snuffing as a metaphor from cattle that dislike their fodder and blow through the nose upon it so that no beast will touch it after, and cites as a complete comment on the curse the history of the couple who kept back part of the price, closing with the observation that it was high time this corrupt service was broken up, God afterwards appearing to pay it no regard. Wesley spreads the blame to the people who learned it by the priests' example, reduces the weariness to the toil of observing every point of the law, and describes the deceiver as the hypocrite who would seem to offer of the best and puts God off with the worst.

Henry will not separate priests from people in the complaint of weariness, both being of that mind, the people grudging the charge of providing the sacrifice and the priests the pains of offering it; they thought the feasts came too thick and the purifying a penance, and it was their own hearts that made a weariness of what God had not. On the curse he meets the point from the other side, that where the person is not accepted the offering will not be, so it is not enough to do what is good in the matter of it.

debates.question: Whose complaint of weariness is recorded?

positions.position: Either the priests', over a service they thought poorly paid, or the people's, over the carrying of the sacrifice.
Both together, the people grudging the charge and the priests the pains.
The toil and drudgery of observing every point of the law.

debates.question: How is the gesture of contempt to be rendered?

positions.position: As snuffing, a metaphor from cattle that blow through the nose on fodder they dislike.
More simply as puffing at the service, treating with contempt what should have been a privilege.

outliers.claim: Conjectures a motive for offering a stolen animal: it would likely carry a mark making it impossible to sell without risking detection, so the thief makes a virtue of necessity and brings to the altar what he could not otherwise dispose of.

themes: But ye have profaned it, in that ye say, The table of the Lord is polluted; and the fruit thereof, even his meat, is contemptible.

Ye said also, Behold, what a weariness is it! and ye have snuffed at it, saith the Lord of hosts; and ye brought that which was torn, and the lame, and the sick; thus ye brought an offering: should I accept this of your hand? saith the Lord.
